China in Ten Words

* Author | Yu Hua
* Abstract | Framed by ten phrases common in the Chinese vernacular, China in Ten Words uses personal stories and astute analysis to reveal as never before the world's most populous yet oft-misunderstood nation. in "Disparity," for example, Yu Hua illustrates the expanding gaps that separate citizens of the country. In "Copycat," he depicts the escalating trend of piracy and imitation as creative new form of revolutionary action. And in "Bamboozle," he describes the increasingly brazen practices of trickery, fraud, and chicanery that are, he suggests, becoming a way of life at every level of society. Witty, insightful, and courageous, this is a refreshingly candid vision of the "Chinese miracle" and all of its consequences.

Abstract
The world-famous Chinese fiction-writer Yu Hua (1960-) recently published a collection of ten essays, China in Ten Words (November 2011), in which he describes the rapid changes in post-Mao China, compares Cultural Revolution events with contemporary phenomena, remembers the prodemocracy protests of 1989, and ponders the causes of current problems. This article's examination of some literary and extraliterary aspects of the work is enhanced by the insight obtained through my encounter with Yu and his presentations in the U.S. Yu has started to speak out publicly, criticizing Chinese official corruption and human rights violations.
